lesson.title: Counting the Currency: Electron Transfer in Redox Reactions
lesson.summary: Every redox reaction moves a specific, countable number of electrons from the reducing agent to the oxidizing agent, and that count is what determines the coefficients in a balanced equation.
lesson.body:
Electrons are the currency of every redox reaction. Once you can count how many electrons a given atom loses or gains, which is just the size of the change in its oxidation number, and you know how many atoms of that element are reacting, you can compute the total number of electrons changing hands. That number is not a side detail, it is the quantity that has to match up between the oxidation half and the reduction half before an equation can be considered balanced.

Try it on a simple example, sodium metal reacting with chlorine gas: 2Na(s) + Cl2(g) is right arrow 2NaCl(s). Split it into half reactions. Sodium: 2Na is right arrow 2Na+ + 2e-, each of the 2 sodium atoms loses 1 electron, for a total of 2 electrons released. Chlorine: Cl2 + 2e- is right arrow 2Cl-, each of the 2 chlorine atoms gains 1 electron, for a total of 2 electrons absorbed. The electrons lost, 2, exactly equal the electrons gained, 2, which is why these coefficients work without needing to multiply either half reaction by anything. Check the final equation: 2 sodium atoms and 2 chlorine atoms on each side, and charge of 0 on the left equal to 2(+1) + 2(-1) = 0 on the right, using the ionic charges inside the neutral formula unit NaCl. Fully balanced.

Now revisit the permanganate and iron equation from a few chapters back, where the finished equation required a coefficient of 5 in front of both Fe2+ and Fe3+. That coefficient was never a guess. Reducing one manganese atom from +7 to +2 requires exactly 5 electrons, while oxidizing one iron atom from +2 to +3 only releases 1 electron, so it takes exactly 5 iron atoms reacting to supply the 5 electrons that one permanganate ion needs. The electron transfer count, 5, is what forces that coefficient into place. Whenever you balance a redox equation and a coefficient looks unusual, like a 5 or an 8, it is almost always electron transfer, not atom counting alone, that put it there.

Since every electron carries a fixed charge of -1, tracking how many electrons move is really the same as tracking how much charge moves from one species to another. That connection between electron transfer and charge is not a coincidence, it is the whole basis for the next idea in this unit, conservation of charge.
